data.title: Infrastructure
data.sentence: Building Blocks of My Productivity Agents

data.title: Guiding principle: contain the Blast Radius
bullets: Never grant agents unrestricted access to your primary machine
Assume things can go wrong: rogue commands, bugs, or unexpected behaviors
Protect against prompt injection triggered during external operations
Prevent data exfiltration and exposure of personal files or credentials
data.speaker_notes: Security is the main reason behind my setup. I don't want to give an autonomous agent full access to my main machine. You always need to contain the blast radius in case something goes wrong—whether it's a security breach, data exfiltration, or a prompt injection triggered while the agent is processing external data.

data.title: Solution: Hermes in a Linux VM

bullets: A self-hosted and dedicated Linux VM on Proxmox
Docker inside the VM for an extra layer of isolation and reproducibility
Strict separation between host OS and agent workspace
Bonus point: VMs are on a separated physical net
CLI-only Linux VM in your machine
GUI Linux / Windows VM in your machine: full desktop environment when visual tools or browsers are needed
Hermes in docker in your machine (mount carefully resources)
Virtual host somewhere
Same core principle: keep the host machine untouched

data.speaker_notes: To achieve this isolation, I run a self-hosted Hermes agent inside a local Linux virtual machine. In my specific setup, I created a Linux VM and put Docker inside it to run the agent. However, you don't necessarily need Docker: you can simply spin up a local VM—either CLI-only or with a full GUI—and run the agent directly inside it.

data.title: Scenarios to Consider
bullets: Managing a single agent
Managing the context of a single agent
Managing multiple isolated agents
Managing multiple interacting agents
data.speaker_notes: When structuring your agent garden, there are several progressive scenarios to consider, from handling a single agent and its context to orchestrating multiple isolated or interacting agents. Each scenario has a specific solution.

data.title: Managing a Single Agent
data.speaker_notes: The Hermes Web Dashboard is the simplest way to access and communicate with Hermes. Beyond offering a chat interface, it also lets you manage all agent configurations in one place. Its biggest advantage is that everything is handled locally, so your privacy stays completely local. The trade-off is figuring out how to reach the host machine remotely, since the dashboard isn't accessible from the outside unless you use an SSH tunnel or configure more advanced networking mechanisms. Still, privacy and simplicity are definitely the key strengths of this first, most immediate solution.

data.title: Managing the Context of a Single Agent
My setup: Discord with multiple agents
data.speaker_notes: I chose Discord for my agent garden for three main reasons: first, it gives me seamless access across both web and mobile through rock-solid client apps; second, it allowed me to bring multiple agents together in the same workspace right from the start; and third, it makes it easy to keep context strictly separated across different conversations using categories, channels, and threads.

data.title: Guiding Principle: Conversation Privacy
bullets: The core criterion for splitting work across agents is conversation privacy
Separate agents based on who has access to the conversation and memory
Prevent context leakage between personal, family, and external interactions
Each agent should only access data it is safe to expose in its channels
data.speaker_notes: The fundamental criterion for choosing how to divide work between a single agent and multiple sub-agents is conversation privacy.
